http://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/0.text: The Ministry of Information of Belarus has designated Euronews’ website as “extremist” media, adding it to its “Republican List of Extremist Materials” following a national court order, according to Belarus-based media outlets.The Euronews website will now be restricted in Belarus, and readers could face administrative penalties for "storing or distributing" its content, after many years in which Euronews has been the main European source of information in the country, according to Euronews’ audience data in Belarus.The state decision was taken by the Horki District Court in the Mogilev Region on 4 August and is "subject to immediate execution in accordance with Article 302 of the Code of Civil Procedure of the Republic of Belarus." Minsk now joins Moscow in banning both Euronews’ television and digital news medias, depriving Belarus audiences of a vital source of factual and independent journalism which also covers Belarus, Russia and the war in Ukraine.Euronews’ Editorial Director Claus Strunz condemned the decision declaring that a state that brands Euronews as “extremist” and blocks access to independent, impartial journalism reveals its own fear of free reporting.”“We have not been informed of this decision and await the authorities’ justification. Our commitment remains unchanged: we stand with our audiences in Belarus and will continue to provide factual, independent journalism guided by our core editorial values,“ Strunz said.Belarus authorities have yet to announce the decision and their arguments that led to this extreme ruling by which Euronews and several other digital medias are now labelled “extremist media” in Belarus.Euronews’ television channel broadcast was banned by Belarus authorities in 2021 on a legal procedural basis, before the Kremlin decided to cut Euronews’ television and digital output across the Russian Federation right after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The independent Belarusian Association of Journalists suggested that the suspension of Euronews broadcasts was linked to attempts to restrict access to sources of information.

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/09/krem.text: Menü Kereső A Kreml az orosz diplomaták kiutasítása ellenére nyitott kapcsolatai fejlesztésére Magyarországgal Külföld Vida Benjámin Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Oroszország megfelelő választ fog adni arra, hogy Magyarország kiutasított tíz orosz diplomatát – közölte Dmitrij Peszkov, az orosz elnök sajtótitkára szerdán Moszkvában. Peszkov így fogalmazott a TASZSZ orosz állami hírügynökség szerint: „Ami konkrétan ezt a döntést illeti, természetesen megfelelő válasz fog születni rá, ezek a lépések nem maradnak válasz nélkül.” Szerinte Magyarország barátságtalan lépései kétségkívül negatívan hatnak majd, és nem lehet, hogy ne járjanak negatív következményekkel a kétoldalú orosz–magyar kapcsolatok egészére nézve. „Nyitottak vagyunk kapcsolataink további fejlesztésére. Ez érdekünkben áll, és nem vagyunk hívei annak, hogy bármilyen kárt okozzunk az orosz–magyar kétoldalú kapcsolataink, mondjuk úgy, értékes örökségében és tapasztalataiban.” Kedden derült ki, hogy a Külügyminisztérium kiutasította Magyarországról az orosz nagykövetség 10 munkatársát is. Orbán Anita külügyminiszter ugyanakkor azt mondta, ez nem jelenti az Oroszországgal fennálló diplomáciai kapcsolatok megszakítását, Magyarország továbbra is fenn kívánja tartani a szükséges párbeszédet a kölcsönös tisztelet és a szabályok betartása mellett. Rácz András, a Magyar Külügyi Intézet vezérigazgató-helyettese azt nyilatkozta, a külügyminiszter nyilatkozatából a diplomáciai nyelvezet szabályai szerint az következik, hogy a Magyarországról kiutasított tíz orosz diplomata valójában diplomáciai fedésben dolgozott, és hírszerzői tevékenységet folytatott. A bejelentés üzenet lehet Oroszországnak arról, hogy új időszak jön, többé Magyarország nem lesz kíméletes az orosz hírszerzőkkel. De az is elképzelhető, hogy ez nem Moszkvának, hanem inkább azoknak a nyugati szövetségeseknek és partnereknek szól, akik már jó ideje nem bíztak a magyarokban. Az orosz külügyminisztérium szóvivője a hírre reagálva „kemény és fájdalmas” választ ígért. „Először is, mi ugyanezt fogjuk tenni. De Magyarország döntése a közös gazdasági projektek csökkenéséhez is vezethet Oroszországgal” – nyilatkozta az orosz TASZSZ hírügynökségnek Alekszej Csepa, az Állami Duma Nemzetközi Ügyek Bizottságának alelnöke. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A tourist golf cart passes in front of the Colosseum. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A tourist golf cart passes in front of the Colosseum. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Italy ‘I have to dodge them all the time’: Rome locals incensed by rise in golf cart tours Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairly Angela Giuffrida in Rome Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end. The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest. View image in fullscreen American tourists Barry and Linda on foot in Piazza Navona. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian “When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”. Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.” For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles. For residents, however, their proliferation in recent years has become another source of frustration in a city already wrestling with traffic and overtourism. View image in fullscreen Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate the carts. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Taxi drivers are especially incensed, accusing golf cart operators of stealing their business, while one local newspaper said the city had been “taken hostage” by the vehicles. Now Rome authorities are cracking down on the burgeoning trade. Police intensified checks this week after the news agency Adnkronos reported that 90% of the roughly 500 golf carts circulating in the city were operating without authorisation. In recent days, police stopped 131 carts around Piazza Navona, the Pantheon, Circo Massimo and the Spanish Steps, issuing €38,000 of fines for offences ranging from unlicensed driving to illegal parking. Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate an activity that “risks spiralling out of control”, Eugenio Patanè, a councillor for mobility, told the news agency Adnkronos. View image in fullscreen A golf cart in traffic in Rome. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Prices vary based on the type of tour and duration, but the cost per person can start at €100 and exceed €400 for a half-day trip. Barry and Linda paid €310 for their three-hour ride. “But it’s worth it,” said Barry. Rome’s traffic problem is hardly new. Julius Caesar tried to tackle the issue more than 2,000 years ago by banning private vehicles and commercial carts from the city’s streets during the day. Today, pedestrians, cars, scooters, delivery vans and the occasional rogue horse-drawn carriage all jostle for space. View image in fullscreen Nora and Carlo outside their shop Trevimage near the Pantheon. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Tourists can also take tours in Fiat 500s, on Vespas with sidecars, and even in tuk-tuks. But the golf carts seem to have drawn a special kind of wrath. “There are too many of them,” said Nora Fahmi, who works at Trevimage, an art photography shop behind the Pantheon. “We’ve had this shop for 13 years and have seen all sorts of things, but the golf cart situation is kind of wild.” Nearby, two teenagers from Israel were taking a rest on a parked cart. “We just want a lift to the Colosseum but you have to book online,” said their mother, Miri. “Rome is too crowded and it’s difficult to walk.” View image in fullscreen Two young tourists rest in a golf cart parked in the town centre. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Elisa Isacco, who lives in the Monti area, spares no sympathy for the weary tourists. “What do they actually see or learn about Rome when they are on one of these things?” she said. “I find myself having to dodge them all the time – Rome is chaotic, it’s like a jungle.” Amid the clampdown, several golf cart tour operators have banned staff from speaking to the press. But Leo Pavoncello, a driver for an operator in the Jewish Ghetto area, was happy to publicly defend the trade. “Golf carts are silent and eco-friendly,” he said. “Rome is not an easy city to visit but these vehicles allow people with disabilities and families with children to see the sites in a comfortable way. On top of that, they provide jobs for young people.” View image in fullscreen A golf cart waiting for a group of tourists in Piazza Navona. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Pavoncello, who was subjected to the police checks and was found to be operating fully legitimately, argued that a few rotten apples were giving the business a bad name. “I don’t understand why they are targeting us,” he said, although he suspects “taxi lobbies” are piling on the pressure. “But Rome is a touristic city that has always been full of traffic, and the golf carts are simply another mode of transport.” Explore more on these topics Italy Overtourism Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
